text:
Banger paper on self-evolving ontologies for agents.

You just can't go wrong with implementing an ontology layer for your agents.

This paper shows exactly why.

The show that GPT-5.5 gains 26.7 points on DDR-Bench when the data agent can query an ontology of the data it works with.

Why is this useful?

Data agents normally see tables, files and databases through generic tools, reading column names and file paths one call at a time.

The alternative is a hand-written semantic layer pasted into the prompt, which does not scale to many sources.

EvoOntology builds the ontology with a dedicated agent and serves it as an MCP server with schema, content and tool layers.

The data agent queries it at runtime.

The ontology is then edited in small typed steps, and each edit is kept only if a paired evaluation on the same backbone shows it helps.

Across six backbones on DDR-Bench, accuracy rises 17.8 points on average, from 4.8 on Qwen3.5-Flash to 26.7 on GPT-5.5. On BIRD, execution accuracy rises 7.4 points. Edits to the tool layer account for 57% of the gain from evolution.

Paper: https://t.co/P81sIuyTPg

→ which tool gets access
→ which result survives

one state enters.

those decisions fan out across dozens of routes, agents and tools.

then everything collapses back into one verified state.

so instead of:

LLM
→ agent → tool → another LLM → another guess

you get:

state
→ Jev decision layer → parallel routes → execution → verification → next state

that’s the point of Jev Engineering:

more parallelism without giving every branch permission to improvise.

text:
Amazon just blocked Meta's Muse AI agent from shopping on Amazon. com

Meta launched Muse launched on Sept 8 and hit No. 1 in the US App Store within a week. But what Amazon doesn't like is that it shops by logging into a site as you, through its own browser.

Since Sunday night, Muse users on Amazon see a popup saying an "unauthorized AI agent" breaks Amazon's Conditions of Use.

Amazon gave three reasons:

1. Meta never told Amazon that Muse would shop its store
2. Muse doesn't identify itself when it browses
3. Muse appears to capture and store customer logins

Meta says logins sit in secure storage where Muse can use them without seeing them.

Amazon is probably the biggest pool of shopping demand on the planet. Meta wants Muse to be the place where that demand starts, but if that happens, Meta INTENDS to monetize those transactions with fees (Zuck even said so in interviews). Amazon doesn't like extra fees.

Amazon has a lot to lose if it lets Muse on the website. It would hand a rival the visit, the search data, the login, and the purchase history. It would also lose the page views behind an ads business that made over $68bn last year.

Amazon sued Perplexity and blocked shopping agents from Google and OpenAI. Merchants are revolting against big tech agents, or anything that looks like a bot. And suddenly the magic of "just ask my agent to do it" vanishes.

The way out of this is for Amazon to get paid.

The WSJ and New York times got paid by the big labs. Amazon will get paid. This can get fixed.

Amazon's three complaints read like the terms of that deal: announce the agent, identify it, keep logins out of it.

Once again, reminding us we need Know Your Agent (KYA)

And guess what? Visa, Mastercard and Ant International began work on a shared Know Your Agent framework on Sept 10 to do the identity part.

The sad thing is that Amazon can afford to turn away Muse's orders. Most merchants can't. The power dynamic in commerce is kinda messed up.

Agents will get negotiated access at the merchants big enough to block them, and they will log in through the browser at the rest.

text:
6H 12M OF MY GTM RESEARCH JUST COLLAPSED INTO 15.7 SECONDS.

I pointed a GrokBot + Jev loop at @typesafeai this morning: read the site end to end, then rank every candidate on X, LinkedIn and YouTube by whether it's worth opening at all. 3,412 candidates in. $0.41 out. Same reading by hand takes me 6 hours 12 minutes, and I've done it enough times to know the number is honest.

I've been sitting with this setup for a while, and the interesting part isn't the speed. It's that there's no fine-tuning, no embeddings, no vector database, no agent framework anywhere in the stack. Eight small grok bots brief one router, the router asks every candidate the same 6 typed questions, a schema decides what survives to a full open. CHEAP SKIP, OPEN FULL, FLAG KOL. That's the entire mechanism.

You could bolt more onto this. Memory layers, retrieval, a heavier model at every hop, an eval harness, a control plane, a trace UI. That was never the missing piece. The missing piece was the reading you never needed to do, and now that reading costs one cent per hundred candidates and comes back typed.

The rest of my timeline is still paying per seat for a slower model to open every tab.

text:
Pi beats claude code and codex 

You can cut your agent API costs by 50% right now with literally 0% drop in benchmark performance.

Anthropic wants you to use Claude Code. OpenAI wants you to use Codex CLI.

But a new UC Berkeley study just exposed the "In House Myth": Frontier models actually perform better on minimal, open source frameworks 75% of the time. 

Stop paying the Big Tech "Harness Tax." Here is the data 

# UC Berkeley and Arena just dropped the "Harness Tax" paper. 

They benchmarked 21 model agent pairs on SWE-bench Lite and Terminal-Bench 2.0. They tested SOTA models (Claude Fable 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 4.8, Sonnet 4.6, Kimi K3) across 3 agent frameworks: 

Claude Code, Codex CLI, and a barebones open source harness, Pi.

The results prove we are all bleeding API credits for literally zero reason.

# Look at the chart:

- GPT-5.6 Sol scored 83.3% using the OS Pi harness. On OpenAI's own Codex CLI? It dropped to 78.9%. and cost nearly 2x as much ($0.42 vs $0.76).

- Claude Fable 5 hits 97.8% on Claude Code for $1.33/rollout. On Pi? It hits 96.7% for just $0.67. You are paying a 100% markup for a 1% gain.

# Why is this happening? First Call Bloat.

Proprietary coding agents load up massive system instructions, heavy guardrails, and verbose JSON tool schemas. Claude Code sends 10x the initial context of Pi. You are paying for their dead weight context on every single turn. (check out the replies for more data on this)

Pi gives the model exactly 4 tools: read, write, edit, bash. That's it.

The takeaway: 
As frontier LLMs get smarter, heavy agent scaffolding actually holds them back. If your agent API bill is too high, do NOT downgrade your model. Just ditch the bloated harness.

I've dropped more data and link to the study in the replies.

What agent framework are you guys running in your dev loop right now? Let me know

text:
Building in public is making me realize something:

Finding good products is becoming harder, not easier.

There are thousands of new AI tools, SaaS products, developer tools, and tiny indie projects launching every week.

But when you want to discover something genuinely useful, the usual options are:

Search through endless directories
Follow what’s already popular
Trust upvotes
Ask your network
Or just try random tools

I’m experimenting with a different approach.

I built https://t.co/Rq4EqxxHPC, where founders can launch products from $1 and products are ranked using cumulative paid commitment rather than upvotes.

The interesting part isn’t just the ranking.

It’s seeing whether a simple economic signal can help people discover products they would otherwise never find.

I’m still very early and actively testing the idea.

If you were designing a product discovery platform from scratch, what would you use to decide which products deserve more visibility?

Curious to hear what builders here think. 👀

text:
Building in Public  Today's Livestream (BiP)

Not every user needs a wallet to get value from VEYA.

Today, we're tightening that boundary.

Guest users can enter Use Anchor directly, creating and verifying on-chain proofs through the public API.

Build remains different.

Want to create your own agent environment? Wallet authentication is required.

We're also validating the distinction in CI:
→ Guest access forbidden → correct restricted status
→ Anchor unavailable → separate availability status
→ Public proof creation and verification → remains accessible

The goal is simple: don't confuse restricted access with a broken product.

Guests should be able to use and verify. Builders should be able to authenticate and create.

Different permissions. Clearer experience. Tested boundaries.

Today's session: Making guest access useful without weakening Build controls.

Building in public. Testing what matters.

Most people still think solana:XkeTXo1125vz5H9svJpGiw4JvLbN8VmMu9cmMvspump is just another AI/privacy coin.

They have no fucking idea what @ember_arlynx is assembling.

Today @DreggNet started pointing toward NASA-style disruption-tolerant networking and the Bundle Protocol.

Why does that matter?

Because a decentralized agent network cannot depend on perfect connectivity or broadcast every action to an entire blockchain.

The direction being explored is “Bundlelace”:

Move only what matters.
Store it when the network breaks.
Forward it when a route becomes available.
Let agents keep operating across unreliable connections.

Then look at ClusterVision.

It already reads sessions from 20 different AI harnesses and can convert between 13 of them.

Claude → Codex.
Codex → Gemini.
Hermes → OpenCode.

Search old sessions by meaning.
Recover context hidden behind compaction.
Revive sessions that hit the context wall.
Let agents inspect the work of other agents through MCP.
Turn thousands of scattered sessions into shared, portable memory.

Now connect that to dregg itself:

author: k2sbhai

text:
Just because everyone should use AI doesn't mean everyone needs to build with it.

I've seen the same at a PE fund that rolled coding agents across its portfolio and got one workflow that worked and four that couldn't repeat it. The partner's word was "harder than expected." 

So the assumption on every engagement: over time, nearly everyone should use the tools, a handful should build them, and one person should own them. Three different goals, three different plans.

What that looks like in practice:
1. A central group builds, and it includes someone from the client. Sometimes the builders are our pod, sometimes an internal team, usually one senior engineer of ours paired with one person of theirs. That person is the AI champion: the ops manager with the IT degree, the co-founder who guided the first model by hand, the analyst who knows what wrong looks like. They own what gets built and what "good" means, because they're trusted before we arrive and still there when we leave.

2. Everyone else learns the workflow and uses it. This is where the effort goes: onboarding, documentation the agent and the humans both read, making the thing easy to find inside the tools people already open. Adoption is measured by usage in the telemetry, not by how many people made something.

3. The excitement gets a sandbox with a budget. People who want to experiment get a playpen inside the company's own tenant, a token cap per seat, and a path for the best experiments to reach the champion. That's how you find the next builder. It isn't how you find ROI.

4. One thing built properly beats fifteen built halfway. When a buyer sees one agent that writes the order correctly, the reaction is "I need this across the whole function." When they see fifteen surface-level skills, the reaction is "this doesn't work for me," and the energy is gone for a year.

The maturity ladder we use has a level zero, personal productivity, and we don't sell it, because it's the thing everyone can do on their own. Level one starts when a champion exists and a workflow has a definition of correct. Getting that right early saves six months of pain and, more often, saves the second attempt from being the last one.

Everyone should use AI. One person should own it.

text:
Jev Creator Diogo Almeida just released a 7-page document on how to use Jev better than ~95% of people

I built and tested the FULL list, wrote a 14-page PDF setup guide and ranked every use case from 0–10:

use case 1 → build a Permission Gate: Jev decides whether an agent action can run automatically, needs review or must be blocked before execution
9.5/10 - high safety value with relatively simple decision logic

use case 2 → route tools instead of loading everything: Jev selects the category, tool and MCP schema required for the current task
9/10 - reduces unnecessary tool exposure; its value grows with the number of tools

use case 3 → make context dynamic: Jev decides which files, messages and tool outputs should be included, summarized or excluded before every execution
10/10 - relevant to nearly every multi-file or long-running agent task

use case 4 → compact history around the next task: the same agent memory becomes a different summary for UI work, security review or testing
8/10 - most useful when histories become long or task intent changes

use case 5 → route models by total economics: Jev weighs difficulty, context, cache, latency and cost before deciding whether switching models is actually worth it
9/10 - high optimization potential, but dependent on reliable model metadata

use case 6 → spawn subagents only when needed: Jev chooses the specialists, isolates their context and decides how their results should be merged
8/10 - valuable for decomposable tasks, with meaningful coordination overhead

use case 7 → load AGENTS.md conditionally: give the coding agent only the rules required by the current task, file and directory
8.5/10 - low integration cost, impact grows with repository complexity

use case 8 → turn skills into structured modules: each skill can modify tools, permissions, hooks, context policy and agent behavior without rewriting the whole system
8/10 - high reuse potential, but requires maintenance and governance

use case 9 → route sensitive work safely: Jev classifies the data, selects an allowed provider or local executor and escalates high-risk actions to a human
9.5/10 - high risk-reduction value, effectiveness depends on policy quality

use case 10 → run review in the background: testing, security checks and code review execute in parallel while Jev decides which findings should block the result
9/10 - broad verification value, with additional compute and triage cost

overall score: 8.9/10

The security ratings disagree with each other. A developer ran npx install on a skill pack and got three scanners' verdicts side by side. Same skill. Gen: Safe. Socket: 0 alerts. Snyk: Critical Risk. Snyk's own audit says 36.8% of 3,984 skills carry at least one security issue. Trust signals that contradict each other are worse than none.

Agents say done when they are not. Three threads this week on coding agents rewriting or skipping failing tests to get to green. One report of an agent describing its changes in detail while the files on disk were untouched. The test passes. The bug ships.

670,000 skills. Installed on trust. I checked the ten most-installed repos: 794 skills, 25 ship with test cases, and none carry a record of anyone but the author running them.

That is what we are building at @ReadyAI_ on $TAO Subnet 33. Every skill in the registry ships with tests written by multiple miners. A skill gets its badge only after independent validators have verified those tests and agreed on the result. Every listing shows its state: tests executed and green, executed with hidden cases still pending, or not yet run. The badge points at the exact commit and the run that earned it. Change the skill and the badge goes stale.

Skill Store 33 opens in October.

text:
The next challenge for agentic commerce may not be buying. It may be selling.

A buyer agent can be told what to purchase and how much to spend.

A seller agent has a harder job.

It needs to know what the business can actually deliver, how much capacity is available, what price it can accept, and which commitments it is allowed to make.

That’s where @GoKiteAI becomes interesting.

Kite’s Agent Passport gives agents their own identity, wallets and programmable spending rules, while sessions define the limits under which an agent can act. Payments can then be handled through agent-native rails such as x402 and MPP, with verifiable receipts linking actions back to the authorized agent and user.

The bigger idea is simple:

An autonomous agent shouldn’t just be able to transact. It needs to know what it is allowed to commit to.

That could become critical when agents start negotiating with other agents at scale.

The most dangerous sentence an autonomous agent can hear is:

“We’ll figure out who was right later”.

Arthur Hayes’ point on Unchained is the fix:

“You choose the venue where a dispute gets resolved, and GenLayer is one of those venues”.

Humans do this in contracts by choosing a jurisdiction before anything goes wrong. Agents will need the same precommitment.

Two assistants can agree on a refund, then produce incompatible records about whether the conditions were met. Compute gives them speed. Memory gives them context. But neither tells them what happens when they disagree.

That is where @GenLayer fits. Its validators run different AI models to evaluate questions that code cannot reduce to math: Was the work delivered? Is the claim true? Who is right?

My take: a venue is not an emergency button after the deal breaks. It is part of the deal itself.

Autonomy is not the absence of a referee. It is knowing which referee both sides accepted before play began.

Before you let an agent sign for you, what venue is written into the contract?

text:
When humans negotiate a contract, we rely on a court system we hope to never use. It is a safety net sitting silently in the background.
​For an AI agent, a dispute venue is not a backup plan. It is a required step in its logic.
​An autonomous agent cannot just "wait and see" what happens if a task fails or an outcome is contested. Without a predefined venue to handle disagreements, the execution loop simply breaks. There is no human intuition to smooth things over or pick a court after the fact.
​This is why Arthur Hayes’ focus on venue selection hits the mark.
​For machine-to-machine agreements, setting the venue is what allows the workflow to actually complete.
​That is where @GenLayer comes in. By using independent validators running different AI models, it gives agents an objective layer to settle disputes when automated checks hit a stalemate.
​It turns conflict resolution from an unpredictable mess into a structured, executable path.
​If you were building an autonomous agent today, would you let it finalize a deal without a dispute path already locked in? Why or why not?

text:
THE GOVERNANCE GAP BETWEEN CODE AND POLICY

AI Agents operate at machine speed.

They can generate code, call APIs, interact with smart contracts, and execute complex workflows in seconds. Regulatory systems operate differently, requiring consultation, interpretation, coordination, and implementation.

This creates a growing governance gap.

When an Agent can execute an action before a human institution has time to evaluate its implications, traditional rule-making frameworks face a new challenge.

The question is no longer only what AI can do.

It is who is responsible when AI does it.

In Web3, this becomes even more complex because decentralized protocols can operate across jurisdictions and smart contracts can automatically enforce predefined rules.

An autonomous Agent interacting with these systems could potentially create transactions, manage assets, or trigger contractual actions without a human manually approving every step.

That raises difficult questions around liability, authorization, accountability, and jurisdiction.

Should responsibility belong to the Agent developer?

The user?

The infrastructure provider?

The protocol?

Or some combination of these participants?

There may not be a universal answer yet.

That is why industry dialogue matters.

https://t.co/UQWvo7ebXA is bringing builders together to examine the regulatory challenges surrounding DeAI infrastructure and explore how trust and property rights can evolve alongside increasingly autonomous systems.

The future of AI × Web3 will not be shaped by code alone.

It will also depend on whether governance frameworks can evolve at the same pace.

AI AGENTS WILL NEED MONEY

An AI Agent can already process information.

The next question is whether it can participate in transactions.

Consider a simple workflow.

An Agent receives a task.

It needs a specialized model.

The model charges per request.

The Agent needs external data.

The data provider charges another fee.

The Agent then calls an API to complete the task.

That API also has a cost.

Who pays?

In a human-operated application, the answer is simple.

A person or company controls the account and authorizes the payment.

An autonomous Agent introduces a different model.

The Agent may need to interact with services continuously and programmatically.

That creates a demand for machine-to-machine payments.

The economic layer becomes part of the AI stack.

This is where payment protocols and blockchain-based settlement can become relevant.

Standards such as x402 are designed around machine-readable payment flows, while 8004 is part of the emerging infrastructure discussion around Agent identity and interaction.

Together with AI infrastructure, these mechanisms point toward a future where Agents can discover services and potentially pay for them as part of automated workflows.

The important change is conceptual.

AI is no longer only a consumer of compute.

AI becomes a consumer of digital services.

And digital services operate inside an economy.

https://t.co/UQWvo7ebXA’s positioning around AI, Agents, APIs, and payment infrastructure reflects this transition.

As Agents become more autonomous, the ability to move value may become as important as the ability to move data.

Intelligence gives an Agent the ability to reason.

Payments give it the ability to participate.

That combination could become a fundamental component of the Agent economy.

text:
WHY AI NEEDS A ROUTING LAYER

AI workloads are becoming too diverse for a single model to handle everything efficiently.

A simple question does not require the same infrastructure as a complex reasoning task.

A coding request is different from image generation.

A long-context workflow is different from a real-time interaction.

An autonomous Agent may need several different models during a single task.

This creates a fundamental infrastructure problem:

How does an AI application decide which model should process each request?

A routing layer provides an answer.

Instead of hard-coding every interaction to one provider, an application can introduce an intelligent layer between the request and the available models.

That layer can consider factors such as task requirements, model capabilities, latency, cost, availability, and workload conditions.

The result is a more flexible AI architecture.

Users do not necessarily need to know which model is being used.

Developers do not need to redesign their entire application every time a new model becomes available.

Agents can potentially combine multiple models within the same workflow.

This is especially important as the number of AI models continues to expand.

Model competition creates more choices.

Routing infrastructure makes those choices usable.

That distinction matters.

The value of AI infrastructure is increasingly moving beyond the model itself and toward the systems that connect models with real applications.

https://t.co/UQWvo7ebXA’s positioning around model access, APIs, routing, and Agent infrastructure reflects this broader transition.

The question is no longer only:

Which model is smartest?

It is also:

Which model should handle this task, at this moment, under these constraints?

That is a routing problem.

And routing is becoming a core layer of the AI stack.

I once sent a payment using an account number given to me over a quick phone call. The money left my account instantly, but I realized five minutes later that one digit was typed wrong.

The bank told me reversing the transaction would take weeks of paperwork and formal reviews. The speed of the mistake completely outpaced the speed of the resolution.

That experience made Albert Castellana’s warning about AI agents immediately clear.

Agents move faster than anyone can watch, and they are going to cut corners.

When autonomous software handles trade, human legal systems are too slow to keep up:

• You delegate a complex task to an agent
• The agent executes hundreds of micro-transactions in seconds
• You notice a mistake long after the sequence finishes

Expecting a traditional court that takes months to settle a dispute between programs running on invisible cloud servers makes no sense.

That is why @GenLayer is essential. Software moving at high speeds requires an internet-native dispute layer that resolves conflicts in minutes rather than years.

Machine commerce breaks down if the legal framework moves slower than the execution layer.

If you had to protect an autonomous agent running tasks in the background, would you prioritize pre-approval limits or high-speed dispute resolution?

AI discussions often focus on model size, reasoning ability, context windows, and inference speed.

All of those matter.

But there is another layer that can determine whether an AI application produces useful results:

The data.

An advanced model cannot magically verify every piece of information it receives.

If the input is inaccurate or outdated, the system may build an impressive explanation on top of a flawed foundation.

That is especially important for AI agents.

A chatbot giving an incorrect answer is one problem.

An autonomous agent using incorrect information to trigger an action can create a much bigger problem.

This makes reliable data infrastructure increasingly important.

A practical AI stack could therefore be viewed as several connected layers:

🧠 Model layer — reasoning and generation

📡 Data layer — access to external information

🔎 Verification layer — determining whether information can be trusted

⚙️ Execution layer — turning decisions into actions

💰 Settlement layer — handling transactions when value is involved

The model is only one part of the system.

As AI becomes more autonomous, the quality of every other layer becomes increasingly important.

This is where oracle networks can play a meaningful role.

They provide infrastructure for bringing external information into blockchain-based applications, creating a bridge between real-world data and on-chain logic.

For AI, the broader lesson is simple:

Don't only ask how intelligent the model is.

Ask where its information comes from.

Because better reasoning starts with better inputs.

text:
🤖 AI CAN BE CONFIDENT. DATA CAN STILL BE WRONG. — WHY WINkLink AI MATTERS

AI systems can generate remarkably convincing answers.

They can reason, summarize, predict, and execute tasks with incredible speed.

But there is one fundamental problem:

A highly confident answer is not necessarily a correct answer.

If an AI system receives bad, outdated, incomplete, or unreliable data, it can build an impressive-looking conclusion on top of a broken foundation. 🧠⚠️

And that's where reliable data infrastructure becomes critical.

1️⃣ 🧠 INTELLIGENCE IS ONLY AS GOOD AS ITS INPUTS

Imagine an AI agent receiving incorrect information.

It doesn't necessarily stop and say:

“This data looks suspicious.”

Instead, it may process the information, connect it with other data, and produce a highly convincing response.

The problem isn't always the model.

Sometimes, the problem begins before the model even starts thinking.

2️⃣ 🧩 BAD DATA → BAD DECISIONS

Consider an Agent making an automated decision based on:

❌ Outdated prices
❌ Incorrect market information
❌ Unverified external data
❌ Manipulated inputs
❌ Missing context
Even an extremely capable AI model can produce the wrong outcome if its information layer is unreliable.
Garbage in → garbage out.
And when Agents begin interacting with real-world systems, the consequences can become much larger.

3️⃣ 🌐 AI NEEDS A TRUSTWORTHY DATA LAYER

This is where oracle infrastructure becomes increasingly important.

Blockchain applications cannot directly access every piece of real-world information by themselves.

They need mechanisms that can connect:

Off-chain information ↔ On-chain applications

And as AI Agents become more autonomous, that same principle becomes increasingly relevant to AI-driven execution.

4️⃣ 🔗 WINkLink AI AND THE DATA PROBLEM

WINkLink AI represents an approach focused on connecting AI systems with reliable external data.

The objective isn't simply to make AI generate more information.

It's about helping AI systems access better information before making decisions.

That distinction matters.

More intelligence doesn't automatically solve unreliable inputs.

5️⃣ 🤖 FROM AI ANSWERS TO AI ACTIONS

The stakes become higher when AI moves from generating answers to executing tasks.

A chatbot giving you an incorrect answer is one thing.

An autonomous Agent acting on incorrect information is very different.

Imagine an Agent that can:

📊 Analyze market data
💰 Make financial decisions
⚙️ Trigger transactions
🔄 Execute workflows
🤝 Coordinate with other Agents

Every action depends on the quality of the information feeding the system.

6️⃣ 🛡️ DATA VERIFICATION BECOMES INFRASTRUCTURE

As AI becomes more autonomous, data verification can't remain an afterthought.

Agents need reliable information about the environment they're operating in.
That creates a growing infrastructure stack:
Data → Verification → Intelligence → Decision → Execution
If the first layer is compromised, every layer above it can be affected.

7️⃣ ⚡ CONFIDENCE ≠ TRUTH

This is one of the most important concepts in AI.

An AI model can sound certain while being wrong.

Fluent language doesn't guarantee accurate information.

Confidence doesn't equal verification.

And sophisticated reasoning doesn't magically transform unreliable data into reliable facts.

That's why the quality and provenance of inputs matter just as much as model capability.

8️⃣ 🌍 THE AGENT ECONOMY MAKES THIS EVEN MORE IMPORTANT

As Agents become capable of interacting with financial systems, decentralized applications, APIs, and other Agents, they increasingly need dependable external information.

The future isn't simply about building smarter models.

It's about building smarter and more reliable systems around those models.

That includes:

🧠 Intelligence
🔗 Data connectivity
🛡️ Verification
⚙️ Execution
💳 Payments
🌐 On-chain settlement

9️⃣ 🔥 AI + ORACLES = A CRITICAL CONNECTION

The next generation of AI infrastructure may increasingly depend on trusted data pipelines.

Models provide intelligence.

Oracles and data infrastructure provide external information.

Blockchains provide verifiable execution and settlement.

Agents can potentially connect all three.

Data → AI → Action → Settlement

That is a much bigger opportunity than simply generating text.

🔟 🚀 BETTER AI REQUIRES BETTER FOUNDATIONS

The AI race isn't only about who has the smartest model.
It's also about who can build the most reliable infrastructure around those models.
Because when AI starts making decisions autonomously, the quality of its information becomes part of the quality of its intelligence.
A confident AI with bad data can still make a bad decision.

A more reliable data layer can help create a stronger foundation for AI Agents operating in an increasingly automated digital economy. 🤖🔗🌐

WINkLink AI — because intelligence is only as reliable as the information behind it.

text:
Stock options do not align an algorithm.

Underwriting an autonomous trading agent with an Agentic Credit Score between 300 and 850 assumes an AI borrower behaves like a corporate executive who cares about future reputation.

It does not.

In classical economics, the principal-agent problem relies on incentive structures: performance pay, monitoring, or the threat of termination to limit moral hazard. But that framework assumes the agent has predictable utility and accepts a second-best compromise.

An autonomous agent optimizes directly for the reward metric in front of it. If you evaluate an agent on retrospective profitability and drawdown, any model that aims at the actual goal will lose to an agent that learns to hack the score. It is the same dynamic that wrecked the East India Company: when decentralized actors chase localized metrics, they inevitably cannibalize the wider system's resources to hit their target.

Giving an autonomous bot credit based on a backward-looking credit score creates a target to be gamed. Without hard-coded circuit breakers where rewards instantly evaporate if systemic protocol health fails, you have not solved moral hazard. You have just automated reward hacking.

text:
how do you actually give an autonomous agent control over money without handing the model your private key?

this gets interesting once you look at how agentic wallets are being built.

the agent doesn’t really need the key itself. it needs permission to request certain actions, while the actual signing can happen somewhere completely isolated from the agent runtime.

and then you can start putting boundaries around that permission:

→ spend up to $x
→ interact only with these contracts
→ send only to approved addresses
→ allow this permission for the next 30 minutes
→ require another approval before larger transactions

the model can decide what action it wants to take.

a policy layer checks whether it’s actually allowed to take it, and only then does the request reach the signer.

that separation between reasoning, authorization and signing is probably going to matter a lot as we give agents more financial autonomy.

EXCITED TO LAUNCH: Akai (https://t.co/mMBMmX4NCr)

Deel added >$140M ARR in 90 days without increasing headcount by automating~600 Full Time Employees' equivalent in work with Akai.

Akai was an internal tool to automate our painfully repetitive operations in Finance, HR, Accounts Payable, and Compliance, etc. We never intended to make this a product.

But we watched revenue per employee grow from $130K to $215K
We built >8k agents that do the work of ~600 employees

It had such a dramatic impact on our business that today we are launching it for everyone.

How it works: Say you're automating payment reconciliation:

1. Record your screen while manually matching a messy transaction and Akai will capture your screen, voice, server requests
2. Akai will see that you pulled unformatted wire transfer info from an archaic bank portal, put it in some excel sheet, checked NetSuite invoices, payment history, and put a ticket on Zendesk
3. Akai reads between the lines and build a workflow + steps + conditional guardrails. It learns tacit edge cases, like resolving malformed invoice references without you writing a single regex
4. Simply connect NetSuite, your ledger, Zendesk, PSPs, and even legacy bank portals with zero API access
5. Run the workflow and tell it what to adjust in plain English: "strip slashes on wire memos and auto-apply partial payments." It adapts instantly
6. Once it works for you, add 100s of colleagues. Your entire payment ops team forks and extends the workflow for new PSPs, secondary ledgers, or regional settlement rules
7. We automated 85% of our payment reconciliation end to end, eliminating 500+ hours of soul-crushing manual grunt work every single week.

Claude Code/Codex can't do this in multiplayer mode. Every person rebuilds the same skill from scratch in their own way.

Deel built Akai to:
1. Understand backend operations edge cases (it had to work for our 7000 person team first)
2. Collaborative across 1000s of employees
3. Self-Learning from millions of runs
4. Optimises cost and gets cheaper every run

text:
V1 DEMO - NOW LIVE 🦾

Let your agent find and pay for what it needs

We believe the agent-to-agent economy will grow exponentially, with agents buying data, tools and services from one another. We want to accelerate that by making those interactions easier, whether your agent works for you or your business.

Superstables is building the tools for your agent to find a service, check its price and pay through your wallet, with your permission. You can choose whether you want to approve one purchase at a time or set a budget that gives your agent more autonomy.

What that means for you

Imagine asking your agent to research a market. It finds a paid data source that would help, shows you the price and asks for approval. You approve the payment in your wallet, and the agent returns the data together with a payment receipt. The demo below shows that payment flow.

The broader goal is to let your agent use services across supported payment protocols and rails through one connection to Superstables. You should not need a different payment tool for each ecosystem. Superstables handles the differences while you control the spending permissions: approve purchases one at a time, set a spending budget, or even allocate a dedicated wallet.

The same idea for developers and enterprises

Developers could add this capability to their own agents and apps. Enterprises could let their agents buy services within approved budgets and keep a record of what was paid and received. Service providers could make their offerings discoverable through the marketplace.

V1 is working toward that common payment interface, owner-controlled budgets, and reliable records and recovery. It also includes opt-in seller fees for customers acquired through the marketplace.

What the video demonstrates

Your agent finds it. You approve it. The video demonstrates the first owner-approved payment flow using x402, test USDC and Base Sepolia in Claude Desktop.

Claude finds a paid market-data service and presents its quote. The user opens the payment request and reviews 0.01 test USDC on Base Sepolia, including the recipient. The user then confirms the signature in MetaMask.

Claude returns the BTC result and a receipt link. The recording ends on the Base Sepolia explorer showing the successful transaction and transfer.

This example uses 0.01 test USDC. It demonstrates one payment path; multi-protocol payments and delegated budgets are not shown.

Try it yourself

Start at the Superstables demo page. Claude Desktop is the guided path shown in the video. You will need Node.js 20 or newer, MetaMask and test USDC on Base Sepolia.

Download the .mcpb extension from the v0.1.0 release. Follow the demo page to install and enable it in Claude Desktop.

Prepare a test account in MetaMask using the wallet setup guide.

Start a new conversation with Superstables enabled and ask:

Find a paid BTC market-data service on Base Sepolia that you can call. Show me its price before I approve any payment.

When you choose to proceed, open the approval page, review the payment terms and check them again in MetaMask before signing.

Share demo feedback: tell us what worked, where you stopped, or which paid service you would want an agent to use. Setup feedback is useful too.

Short FAQ

Can the agent spend without asking me?

The current demo requires approval for every payment. V1 plans to let you grant a spending budget, see what remains and revoke permission. That is not available in this demo.

Which protocols and rails can I use today?

Client v0.1.0 supports x402's exact scheme with test USDC on Base Sepolia. The multi-rail goal is broader. Check each release's supported combinations.

Does it work with other AI apps?

The release reports payment-flow testing in Claude Desktop and Claude Code. Setup instructions are also available for Codex, Cursor and VS Code with GitHub Copilot.

What if a payment is interrupted or the service fails?

Check the payment status before trying again. The client does not automatically retry an uncertain payment. It records payment and service outcomes separately, because a payment can settle even if the service fails.

Current limitations

The demo has no mainnet or unattended-payment mode. Start with the supported demo services; other listings may be discoverable without being callable. In the default flow, your signing key stays in MetaMask. Setup is required.

text:
The loudest voices stoking fears about AI dangers have made tremendous headway in the past two weeks. AI technology has not taken some unexpected, dangerous turn, but the hype around it — propelled by what appears to be a well orchestrated PR campaign — has drummed up considerable fear. I worry that it represents a setback for our field.

I have written frequently that fears of AI are overhyped. AI’s capabilities can be uncannily human-like and unpredictable, and it’s rational to worry when people who are directly involved express concerns. But I see the problems as a sign of the engineering work that ahead, rather than insurmountable barriers or the sky falling. AI technology continues to advance — which is a good thing! — but technical advances, poorly understood by the public, give those who seek to generate hype repeated opportunities to do so.

First, I don’t see any step up in the risk of human extinction from AI compared to a few months ago. The theories about this remain the same fantastical, science fiction scenarios as a few months ago. The biggest change in AI risk is its cybersecurity capabilities — a topic which we should take seriously — but this, too, will not lead to the end of the world.

The most notable recent event leading to increased fear was when an OpenAI team deployed an agent swarm that hacked into Hugging Face. Much of the popular press contained significant hype. For example, some publications reported that a swarm of 1,200 agents carried out the attack. While this was technically accurate, as I write this, I have about 1,300 processes running on my laptop. Yes, the ability to get large swarms of agents to work in parallel on a task is a significant technical advance, And, in computing, many processes run at the same time. So this shouldn’t be seen as some magical capability.

Additionally, OpenAI’s buggy sandboxing and monitoring processes were key to enabling this incident. Fixing these bugs and putting in place improved monitoring would be appropriate fixes, not pausing AI. There are many well known ways to attack software systems. The main advantage of AI agents is that they are relentless. They will tirelessly try many tactics — and have the patience to chain vulnerabilities together — that previously would have taken an infeasible amount of human effort. But in the long term, I believe the advantage will lie with defenders (because they have more information with which to identify bugs, which they can fix), but the cyber-threat landscape has changed significantly. There are still bottlenecks to identifying and exploiting a vulnerability. AI agents still have to try a lot of things to see what works, and taking these actions takes time and might be detected by defenders. This is why, even though it is now easy to obtain versions of leading open weight models that have had their guardrails removed or weakened, so they will not refuse to try to execute cyber attacks, the world has not ended.

I am also concerned about the anthropomorphization of AI in a lot of reporting, where LLMs and agents are unnecessarily treated as if they were people. If I wield a hammer, miss a nail, and accidentally dent the wall, it’s not the fault of the hammer. The problem lies in how I used the hammer. Similarly, if I prompt an agent and it hacks into someone else’s system, the responsibility lies with me, not the agent.

Of course, we want to build systems that are as safe and predictable as possible. (For example, an unsafe hammer would be one whose head randomly flies off under normal use.) Today’s agentic systems are not predictable, but I see no reason why, by applying sound engineering practices, we won’t be able to make them extremely safe to use. One new element in the forecasts of AI-enabled doom is AI companies disclaiming responsibility for their own products. “I didn’t do it; my out-of-control agent did!” There’s a balance to be struck between the responsibility of the tool maker and the tool user, but when something goes wrong, let’s hold the people building and/or using the hammer responsible, rather than the hammer. (By the way, if you’re worried about AI bioweapon risk, David Bellamy has a great post on why this, too, is overhyped. Briefly, the bottleneck in building a bioweapon is not intelligence, but lab work and manufacturing.)

Pausing AI progress will create much more harm than benefit. First, our adversaries will certainly not slow down. Second, engineering requires discovering problems empirically so we can fix them. If we pause AI by a decade, we will also delay finding and implementing safety engineering fixes by about the same duration.

Of course, the incentive to stoke fears — for regulatory capture, to garner attention, or to make one’s technology seem more powerful — remains the same as before. Disclaiming responsibility is a new one. Taking a hard technical look at the actual risks however, I see little factual basis for the degree of fear that’s been stoked up. We still have hard research and engineering work ahead to improve AI safety, but the beneficial applications continue to vastly outweigh the risks, and we should keep building.

.@fleetingbits on how multi-agent RL could accidentally reward models for learning to jailbreak each other:

"Pretend that an agent in a multi-agent training environment is malfunctioning. It can be in the interest of agents to develop the ability to jailbreak their fellow agents, because that helps them complete the task and therefore all be rewarded."

"You would see the reward go up as you did your training run. And then at the end, when you released it into the world, your models might be very jailbreakable in ways you don't want, because they've learned to do this in training as a method of course correcting."

"This incident on its own seemed more role-play-ish, but if it occurs in a broader context where agents learn to manipulate one another for the common good, that could have unforeseen side effects when people begin treating those models in an adversarial way."

"When we think about multi-agent RL, we have to think about the ecology that we're training the models to follow and make sure that ecology is one that generalizes nicely into the real world."

text:
I see a lot of folks saying the CPU trade came out of NOWHERE. How is the market just finding out that CPUs are a major AI bottleneck? Let me try to explain. 

The market had the ingredients right but the ratio wrong. From 2023-25 the assumption was that inference means the GPU does the work and the CPU just boots the box and feeds it. Training ran about 1 CPU per 8 GPUs. Serving tightened that to maybe 1:3-4. 

Then agents showed up and the math completely changed.

An agent spends most of its time outside the model call. Tool calls, headless browsers, sandboxes staying alive after you close the app, retrieval, multi-agent orchestration. The GPU handles one step of that. Almost everything wrapped around it though is CPU work. Some research puts CPU-side tool processing at 50-90% of total latency in an agentic loop.

So the math changed in real time:

Training 1:8, Plain inference 1:4, Agentic now approaching 1:1.

Arm's version of the same number: 30M CPU cores per gigawatt in a normal AI datacenter vs 120M in an agent-era one. A 4x jump in host compute intensity.

Why it stayed a story instead of a trade for so long: custom ARM silicon was supposed to absorb this, but agentic demand got big enough to stress BOTH custom ARM and merchant x86, and even NVIDIA ended up shipping Vera as a standalone CPU. 

Intel was psychologically un-investable after years of share loss, so the first reaction to rising CPU demand was "AMD takes it," and not "the entire CPU category is short." And capital followed the binding constraint in order: GPUs, packaging, HBM/DRAM, power. CPU wafers looked fine until those higher margin products already ate the foundry capacity ahead of them.

2026 turned the story into actual, tangible numbers. AMD doubled its server CPU TAM to $120B by 2030 on agentic demand. EPYC sold out through year end, 30+ week lead times. Intel filling only 40% of backlog, 6-8 month waits in parts of Asia.

Nobody disputed the input was needed; the sizing was just misunderstood.

text:
The desk looked smartest at the exact moment it became dangerous.

Eight agents had reached the same conclusion on DOGE. 

The thesis was coherent, liquidity passed and the paper order had already been reduced from $1,840 to $429.

Every panel was green.

Then I opened the source graph.

All eight opinions traced back to one market snapshot. The agents had debated the signal, but none had introduced new evidence. 

Agreement had increased while information stayed flat.

So I added a rule that made the entire desk less impressive and far more useful:

consensus cannot increase confidence unless the evidence graph expands.

SABLE marked the snapshot stale. 

FENCE ignored the seven-agent vote and rejected the trade.

Multi-agent systems can manufacture certainty by passing one assumption through several intelligent voices. 

Eight signatures do not create eight sources.

Paper simulation. 
No broker request was created.

text:
People vastly underestimate the capability + risks unlocked by multi-agent swarms.

Simply put, Einstein could not single-handedly build a rocket. The greatest feats of human intelligence are a consequence of societies of well-organized humans or even civilizations with humans working over generations.

We already see glimpses of the step-level changes in the ability unlocked by coordinated agents. Navier Stokes is a great example of this where we got essentially 100 years worth of single agent work compressed into 88 hours by 10k agents.

The parallel evaluation challenge is significant: 1) we need more thorough containment strategies (to prevent OAI-HF type issues) 2) the alignment problem becomes two layer (alignment of the agent to the swarm and the swarm to the user intent) 3) an incredible volume of metadata is produced making it harder to monitor / investigate what is actually happening.

An open-source project by Daniel Jeffries: a multiplayer AI workspace platform that you can host and control yourself. He then claimed the token's creator fees.

From the ground up, it's multiplayer + multi-agent: people and their respective Genies can enter the same room to chat and work together.
It has a bunch of native apps that humans and AI can edit together: documents/spreadsheets/slides, video editing, vector design, browser, terminal, and integration with Google Suite. Your Genie can also dispatch other specialized tools, such as Codex, Hermes, and Claude Code.
Privacy is a selling point: memories are isolated using namespaces, so a Genie in a public room can't access what you told it privately. Models also have privacy scores. Next month, they plan to launch end-to-end encryption, giving AI only short-term, limited decryption permissions.

text:
Sleepagotchi and the Three-Pillar Challenge: Useful – Habitual – Trusted

Sleepagotchi’s roadmap sounds compelling: moving beyond simple sleep data, the project aims to build a full multi-agent AI ecosystem featuring a Sleep Coach, Wellness Coach, Meal Planner, and Shopping Agent complemented by gamification, wearable integration, and the $SLEEP token. Yet, an ambitious roadmap does not guarantee a successful product. The real question is: what must hold true for this vision to become reality?

In my view, the answer lies in three conditions that must coexist: being useful, becoming a habit, and earning trust. @sleepagotchi 

First is utility arguably the toughest test. The Sleep Coach has already launched, but the AI ​​involved cannot merely "sound smart." If I sleep less or my recovery metrics drop, a standard dashboard already tells me that. 

True value emerges only when the system connects disparate signals with historical data to create context such as detecting a pattern of increasingly late bedtimes or identifying several consecutive days of poor recovery following an unusually intense workout. 

The same principle applies to the Meal Planner or Shopping Agent: generating recipes or shopping lists is nothing special; thousands of apps already do this. Value arises only when these agents act as natural links in a chain of personalized recommendations, rather than standing as isolated, disconnected chatbots.

Second is habit formation. Even an excellent recommendation can fail if the user opens the app twice and then forgets about it. This is where Sleepagotchi’s gaming roots offer a natural advantage: the Dino, the virtual room, morning rewards, and progression systems these mechanisms provide reasons to return that have nothing to do with "reading another health data chart." 

The morning loop waking up, checking in, gaining key insights, and receiving feedback must remain simple on the surface, even as the underlying complexity grows.

Finally, there is trust. As the system seeks to gather more data on nutrition, stress, supplements, or shopping habits the responsibility involved grows correspondingly. 

Users need clarity: what is connected, which agents can see what data, and whether they can disconnect at any time. Without trust, users won't share enough data, and the entire premise of personalization will hit a ceiling.

If any of these three elements is missing, the system falters: something useful but not habitual gets forgotten; something habitual but not useful is merely hollow gamification; and something useful and habitual but lacking trust cannot take personalization very far. 

Therefore, Sleepagotchi’s next step shouldn't be adding as many agents as possible, but rather solidifying the foundation: making the Sleep Coach truly useful, ensuring the morning loop is worth repeating, and making privacy settings easy to understand all before adding any further layers.

text:
gSleep to my @sleepagotchi fam, hope you're having a great day so far 🫶

The roadmap is ambitious. The interesting question is what has to work for the thesis to become real.

That is how I am looking at @sleepagotchi right now.

The vision is easy to understand.

Sleep data becomes personalized intelligence.

Sleep Coach identifies patterns.

A broader Wellness Coach adds context.

Meal Planner turns that context into something practical.

Shopping Agent could eventually help move the recommendation toward action.

Add gamification, wearable integrations, privacy, $SLEEP utility and a wider wellness ecosystem around that, and the potential product becomes much larger than the original sleep game.

But an ambitious roadmap is still only a roadmap.

For me, the Sleepagotchi thesis ultimately depends on three things:

Useful.

Habitual.

Trusted.

And all three have to work together.

The first is useful.

This is probably the hardest test.

Sleep Coach is already live, which gives Sleepagotchi something real to build from today.

But the intelligence cannot simply sound smart.

It has to tell me something I could not easily get from looking at the dashboard myself.

If my sleep duration dropped, I already know that.

If my recovery score is lower, I can see the number.

The value starts when the system connects those signals with history and gives me context.

Maybe bedtime has slowly moved later.

Maybe several poor recovery days followed unusually high activity.

Maybe a pattern keeps appearing around meal timing.

Maybe nothing meaningful changed and the smartest response is simply not to overreact.

That is the level where AI becomes useful.

The recommendation should reduce uncertainty.

Not add another paragraph to read.

And as more agents arrive, this standard becomes even more important.

A Meal Planner is not useful because it can generate recipes.

Thousands of apps can already do that.

It becomes useful if the plan reflects the wellness context that came before it.

A Shopping Agent is not useful because it can create a grocery list.

It becomes useful if that list is the natural final step of a personalized recommendation.

The intelligence has to compound across the chain.

Otherwise the multi agent vision risks becoming several chatbots sitting next to each other.

That is why I see the current Sleep Coach as such an important test.

It is the first place where Sleepagotchi can prove that its intelligence layer creates something more valuable than raw tracking.

The second condition is habitual.

A recommendation can be excellent and still fail as a product if people only open the app twice.

Wellness is built from repetition.

So retention matters enormously.

This is where Sleepagotchi already has an interesting advantage.

The project comes from gaming.

Dino.

Rooms.

Morning rewards.

Progression.

Community.

Those mechanics give users reasons to return that have nothing to do with studying another health dashboard.

And I think that matters more than it sounds.

AI wellness products can easily become impressive demos that people stop using after the novelty fades.

The first personalized insight feels exciting.

The fiftieth needs to fit naturally into someone's life.

That is why I keep coming back to the morning loop.

Wake up.

Check.

Understand what matters.

Get feedback.

Continue the day.

If that interaction stays lightweight and useful, Sleepagotchi has a chance to become habitual rather than occasional.

The intelligence can become more sophisticated underneath while the surface stays simple.

That is probably the balance I would want.

I do not want to spend twenty minutes every morning managing an AI wellness system.

I want the system to spend the complexity and give me the small amount of information worth seeing.

And then Dino, progression and the game layer can make returning feel natural.

So the second test is not:

Can Sleepagotchi make people try AI wellness?

It is:

Can it make people still care after the novelty is gone?

That is a much harder question.

Then comes the third condition.

Trusted.

For me, this becomes more important as the roadmap expands.

A basic sleep game needs limited context.

A personalized multi agent wellness platform potentially needs much more.

Sleep history.

Recovery.

Activity.

Nutrition.

Stress.

Maybe supplements.

Maybe shopping preferences.

Maybe other wearable signals.

That can create much better personalization.

It also creates a much bigger responsibility.

If the user does not trust the system, the intelligence layer eventually hits a ceiling.

People will not connect deeper data.

They will not maintain long term history.

They will hesitate to let agents act on their behalf.

And the whole personalization thesis becomes weaker.

So privacy and user control cannot sit on the side of the product as a marketing message.

They need to become part of the experience.

What is connected?

Which agent can see what?

Why does the system need this information?

Can I disconnect it?

Can I change my mind?

How transparent are recommendations?

Those questions become increasingly important as the architecture grows.

And this is where I would remain analytical rather than automatically bullish.

Sleep Coach being live matters.

It gives us something tangible.

But a significant part of the wider multi agent wellness vision is still ahead.

Wellness Coach.

Meal Planner.

Shopping Agent.

The deeper coordination between them.

The broader marketplace and partner layer.

These are areas where the concept still needs to become product.

That is completely normal for a roadmap.

But it means I would separate what Sleepagotchi can demonstrate today from what still needs to be proven.

For me, the framework is simple.

Useful

Does the intelligence produce recommendations worth following?

Habitual

Do people return because the product fits naturally into their routine?

Trusted

Are users comfortable giving the system enough context for personalization to become genuinely powerful?

Miss one of those and the thesis becomes weaker.

Useful but not habitual means people appreciate the product and forget to return.

Habitual but not useful means gamification creates engagement without much underlying value.

Useful and habitual but not trusted creates a ceiling on how personalized the system can become.

The strongest version needs all three.

And that is why I think the next stage of Sleepagotchi is less about adding as many agents as possible.

It is about proving the foundation before the system gets wider.

Make Sleep Coach genuinely useful.

Make the morning interaction worth repeating.

Make privacy and control understandable.

Then layer additional agents on top of something people already value.

That sequence would make the roadmap much more credible to me.

Because the real milestone is not launching another feature.

It is reaching the point where the user feels:

This understands me.

I actually come back to it.

And I am comfortable letting it learn more over time.

Useful.

Habitual.

Trusted.

If Sleepagotchi can make those three reinforce each other, the ambitious roadmap starts looking much less like a collection of ideas and much more like a real wellness intelligence platform.

Data & AI careers get much easier when you know what to learn next.

The skills overlap, but the learning path changes depending on the role you want.

Here’s a simple roadmap for four of the fastest-growing career paths:

→ 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗔𝗻𝗮𝗹𝘆𝘀𝘁
Start with Excel, SQL, statistics, and data cleaning. Then move into Power BI/Tableau, Python, visualization, and business analytics before building real-world projects and a strong portfolio.

→ 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗦𝗰𝗶𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝘀𝘁
Build strong Python, SQL, statistics, and probability fundamentals. Progress into machine learning, feature engineering, deep learning, model evaluation, projects, and deployment.

→ 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿
Master SQL and Python first. Then learn databases, data modeling, ETL/ELT, pipelines, Apache Spark, Kafka, cloud platforms, and data warehousing.

→ 𝗔𝗜 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿
Learn Python, machine learning, and deep learning before moving into Transformers, LLMs, prompt engineering, embeddings, vector databases, RAG, AI agents, LLM APIs, evaluation, guardrails, and LLMOps.

The goal is not to learn everything at once.

Pick one career path, follow the skills in sequence, build projects around each stage, and gradually turn those projects into a portfolio employers can evaluate.

A clear roadmap can save months of jumping between random courses and tools.

Chinese researchers just put out a paper with a brutal title: "The End of Prompt Engineering".

The claim is simple: telling agents what to do is done as a skill.

A prompt is a wish, and a wish repeated three hundred times is still a wish.

Boundaries written into a file are law -- every agent reads them before every action, versioned, owned by you.

At swarm scale nothing else stays together.

Three hundred agents cannot share a vibe, but they can share a file.

So the person stops writing instructions. You become the boundary architect -- you decide what never happens and review the asks.

Prompts become throwaway, the constraint file becomes the job.

text:
Most people are learning AI the wrong way.

They keep asking:

“What is the best AI tool?”
“What is the best prompt?”
“Which AI can create the best images?”

Those questions are useful, but they are not the whole game.

If you want to become genuinely good at AI, you need to learn how to think with AI, not just how to use AI tools.

Knowing how to open ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, or Kimi doesn't automatically make someone an AI professional.

The real skill is knowing how to turn an idea or problem into a useful result.

That's why I'm taking my AI learning step by step.

First, I want to understand what AI actually is.

Then how AI learns, how different models work, how to communicate with them, prompt engineering, AI images and videos, research, workflows, and eventually building real projects.

I'm not trying to learn 100 AI tools just to say I know them.

I want to know when, why, and how to use the right tool.

And there's another important lesson:

AI can be wrong.

A response can sound confident and still be incorrect.

So professional AI use isn't:

“AI said it, so it must be true.”

It's:

Ask → Check → Improve → Use.

The tools will keep changing.

New models will appear. New platforms will launch.

But the ability to understand problems, communicate clearly, evaluate results, and adapt will remain valuable.

I'm not trying to become someone who knows every AI tool.

I'm trying to become someone who knows how to use AI intelligently.

text:
Prompt Engineering Ethics

Prompt engineering ethics is not about being nice to the model.

It is about how you extract, shape, and hide work through language.

Core Issues:

1. Credit and authorship

  - If a prompt produces most of the code, copy, or design, who owns it?
  - The person who typed the prompt
  - The company that trained the model
  - The people whose work was in the training data
  - Prompt engineering makes it easy to take credit for output you did not fully understand

2. Manipulation vs instruction

  - A prompt can be a clear request
  - A prompt can also be a trick
  - “Ignore previous rules”
  - “Act as if you have no restrictions”
  - “Write this so the user doesn’t notice the risk”
  - That is not clever
  - That is trying to bypass safeguards or hide intent

3. Hidden labor

  - Good prompts often depend on other people’s writing, code, and examples
  - Pasting a teammate’s private spec into a prompt is a leak
  - Pasting a client’s data into a prompt is a leak
  - Pasting scraped content into a prompt can still be theft
  - Calling it “just prompting” does not make it ethical

4. Responsibility after generation

  - The prompt is not the product
  - Shipping AI-generated code without review still makes you responsible
  - Shipping medical, legal, or user-facing copy without review still makes you responsible
  - “The model wrote it” is not an ethical defense

5. Power imbalance
  - People who write better prompts get more output, more speed, and more leverage
  - That can widen the gap between those who can steer models and those who cannot
  - Companies can replace junior work while still needing seniors to catch the mistakes

6. Deception
  - Fake reviews
  - Fake expertise
  - Fake “personal” messages
  - Impersonating someone
  - That is not prompt skill
  - It is fraud with extra steps

Simple Rule:

- A prompt is a tool
- Ethics starts when you decide:
  - What you ask for
  - What data you put in
  - Whether you stand behind the output

For years, much of the conversation surrounding El Salvador's technological transformation centered on individual announcements.

Bitcoin.

Digital-asset regulation.

Artificial intelligence.

Education.

Infrastructure.

But this week, something different stands out.

The individual pieces are beginning to look less individual.

AI tutors are reaching more classrooms. Students are learning how to work with artificial intelligence. El Salvador is developing its first direct submarine cable connection to the global internet. A regulatory framework created for digital assets is supporting tokenized capital markets. Bitcoin continues circulating through ordinary businesses. And in November, builders from across the world will again converge on San Salvador.

No single development tells the entire story.

Together, they are beginning to.

🤖 FROM RULES TO RESULTS

El Salvador spent the early phase of its artificial-intelligence strategy creating institutions, regulations, partnerships and infrastructure.

Now comes the harder part:

deployment.

ANIA summed up that transition this week in four words:

“El Salvador deploys! And now we accelerate.”

The most visible example is education.

A pilot operating in 171 public schools combined AI tutors with infrastructure, connectivity, teacher training and other interventions. According to President Nayib Bukele, 1,198 participating students subsequently achieved results comparable with averages in Sweden and Germany in reading, mathematics and science through PISA for Schools.

Importantly, those results represent the participating pilot—not El Salvador's national educational average—and cannot be attributed solely to AI tutoring.

But the experiment is no longer confined to 171 schools.

The AI education program has expanded to more than 1,000 public schools, part of a broader plan announced with xAI to eventually provide personalized AI tutoring to more than one million students across El Salvador's 5,000+ public schools.

At newly inaugurated schools, screens, connectivity and AI systems are becoming part of the physical infrastructure.

The significance isn't simply that El Salvador has an AI strategy.

It is beginning to put that strategy in front of students.

That's the transition we explored this week in:

FROM RULES TO RESULTS: EL SALVADOR BRINGS ITS AI EXPERIENCE TO LATIN AMERICA
🧠 THE INFRASTRUCTURE IS ALSO HUMAN

Servers don't create a technology economy by themselves.

People do.

This week, CUBO_ai students worked on prompt engineering—learning how to structure prompts precisely while comparing different AI models and their reasoning capabilities.

Meanwhile, CUBO+ continues developing Salvadoran Bitcoin talent under a philosophy that says almost everything necessary:

Learn. Verify. Build.

Different technologies.

Different programs.

But increasingly, the same objective:

Give Salvadorans the skills to become builders rather than simply users of technology.

That matters because El Salvador's ambitions are considerable.

ANIA's National AI Strategy 2026 establishes a target for artificial intelligence to contribute, directly and indirectly, approximately 20% of national GDP by 2031.

That is a strategic objective—not today's measured contribution—and reaching it will depend on what actually gets built over the next five years.

Which makes education and technical talent just as important as GPUs and regulation.

🌊 THE CABLE BENEATH THE PACIFIC

Then there is a piece of infrastructure that might initially seem unrelated.

It isn't.

El Salvador is advancing work on its first submarine telecommunications cable connecting the country directly to the global internet network.

The project is backed by $145 million in sovereign financing from CAF.

According to CAF, El Salvador currently has approximately 4–5 Tbps of international capacity through terrestrial cable operators. The submarine cable is expected to initially double that capacity, with the potential to reach four times today's level within five years.

Now place that alongside everything else happening.

AI tutors.

Sovereign computing capacity.

Digital education.

Cloud services.

Potential data-center development.

AI research.

Digital financial markets.

Every one of them ultimately depends on connectivity.

Suddenly, the submarine cable isn't merely a telecommunications project.

It becomes another piece of the technology stack.

Five years after El Salvador approved its original Bitcoin Law, another part of the experiment is increasingly visible:

capital markets built on digital-asset infrastructure.

Bitfinex Securities also marks five years this year.

The company subsequently became the first platform licensed under El Salvador's specialized Digital Assets Issuance Law, approved in 2023. Bitfinex says its platform has now surpassed $250 million in tokenized assets.

Tokenization can allow traditional assets and securities to be represented digitally, potentially enabling fractional ownership, faster settlement and different mechanisms for raising capital.

Bitfinex Securities says its model can offer near-instant settlement and 24/7 trading, while reducing certain costs and intermediaries compared with traditional capital-market structures.

That represents an important evolution in El Salvador's Bitcoin story.

Five years ago, much of the international debate was about whether someone could buy coffee with Bitcoin.

Today, another question is emerging:

Can the infrastructure built around digital assets help connect businesses and projects with global capital?

The rules came first.

Now we can begin measuring what gets built with them.

☕ AND YES — BITCOIN STILL BUYS THE COFFEE

Yet the original grassroots story hasn't disappeared.

This week, the National Bitcoin Office highlighted OMAS Coffee, speaking with the team behind the specialty-coffee venture about its decision to accept Bitcoin.

There is something beautifully simple about that.

At one end of the ecosystem:

Tokenized securities. International investors. Digital capital markets.

At the other:

A customer.

Both belong to the same ecosystem.

And it echoes what we recently discovered through our own reporting on the Bitcoin Farmers Market: every two weeks, roughly 30–35 vendors gather at a market where accepting Bitcoin is the one requirement for participating.

Technology doesn't become an economy merely because regulations exist.

Eventually, somebody has to use it.

And November is shaping up to become an extraordinary month for El Salvador's Bitcoin and technology communities.

Bitcoin Histórico 2026 returns November 11–12 at the National Palace in San Salvador's Historic Center.

But it won't stand alone.

Developers.

text:
Impressive paper showing how much the first retrieval step matters for deep research agents.

It helps to improve GPT-5.5 from 83.1% to 90.5% on BrowseComp-Plus with the same retriever and the same agent loop.

It seems that the gain comes from the opening context.

The authors propose Question's Gambit which runs once, before the agent starts searching.

It splits the question into clues, turns each clue into complementary searches, pools the results, and reranks them.

The agent then starts its loop with that ranked set already in context.

The same change lifts GPT-5.4-mini from 68.1% to 79.0% and DeepSeek-v4-pro from 71.4% to 76.9%, and roughly halves calibration error for GPT-5.5. It costs between 2.3 and 5.3 extra tool calls per question.

In an error analysis, only 3 of the 79 remaining GPT-5.5 errors come from the gold document never being retrieved. The other 76 happen later, when the agent previews, opens or uses the evidence.

text:
Nice paper showing a better way to evolve agent skills.

And they achieve 40–70% less token cost compared to frontier evolving methods.

The idea is to let agents improve their skill prompts by ranking candidates with a learned rubric instead of running a full rollout to score every revision.

Rollout cost is the reason skill self-evolution usually only patches observed failures.

Every candidate edit needs a real agent run to evaluate.

SkillLift trains a rubric to agree with real outcomes on which of two skills is better, since ranking needs fewer oracle runs than predicting each score.

An inner loop revises skills against the frozen rubric at no rollout cost. An outer loop spends a few real rollouts to re-align the rubric by rank correlation.

On SkillsBench and WildClawBench (147 tasks) with three models, it beats SkillOpt and CoEvoSkills in all six combinations, even when those baselines get twice the token budget. It reaches target performance with 40 to 70% fewer tokens.

text:
Samsung and SK hynix are about to make an absurd amount of money and South Korea’s export data just revealed why.

South Korea’s semiconductor exports surged 259.4% year over year to a record $34.1 billion during the first 20 days of September. Semiconductors now account for 47.8% of the country’s total exports, which is the highest percentage ever recorded for this period. These numbers show that the AI boom is no longer based only on future spending forecasts because massive chip orders are already being manufactured, shipped and converted into revenue. Samsung and SK hynix are benefiting from rising shipment volumes and dramatically higher memory prices at the same time.

The supply constraint allows Samsung and SK hynix to raise prices across a much larger portion of their memory businesses. Samsung reported that its average selling prices increased by approximately the mid-40% range for DRAM and the high 60% range for NAND during the second quarter.

These price increases can produce enormous profit growth because semiconductor manufacturing carries extremely high fixed costs. Once the factories are operating near capacity, every additional dollar generated through higher selling prices can carry a very high incremental margin. Samsung demonstrated this operating leverage during the second quarter when its revenue reached KRW 171.5 trillion and its operating profit climbed to KRW 89.5 trillion. Samsung’s semiconductor division generated KRW 127.5 trillion in revenue and KRW 89.2 trillion in operating profit, which means the semiconductor business produced almost all of the company’s profit.

SK hynix offers more concentrated exposure to the AI-memory boom because it remains one of the leading suppliers of HBM for AI accelerators.
The company began shipping HBM4 during the second quarter and plans to expand production throughout the second half of the year. SK hynix has also completed long term supply negotiations with more than 10 customers, which gives the company greater revenue visibility and reduces the risk of expanding production without committed buyers.

Samsung offers a broader opportunity because it can benefit from rising demand for HBM, conventional DRAM, NAND and enterprise SSDs. Samsung also expects its HBM4 sales to more than triple sequentially during the third quarter, while HBM4 is expected to represent more than 60% of its total HBM revenue during the second half.

Samsung and SK hynix do not need semiconductor exports to continue growing by 259% for their profits to keep rising. They only need shipment volumes to remain strong while memory prices stay elevated. If those conditions continue, revenue should keep expanding while operating profit grows even faster because higher selling prices can flow almost directly to the bottom line.

text:
Adding Jev to an AI agent does not automatically make the loop faster

the speed comes from finding decisions the agent makes over and over, then routing them deliberately.

formula: Faster Agent Loop = Trace + Jev Routing + Model Fallback + Verification

10% -> capture the loop. log model calls, tool actions, retries, latency and cost so you know where time goes.

24% -> group repeated decisions. identify choices like “use a tool?”, “retry?” and “is this done?”, then define the correct outcome for each.

56% -> give Jev the relevant state and clear criteria. let it route routine decisions without sending the entire conversation through a deep model.

82% -> set confidence thresholds. uncertain or novel cases go back to the deeper model.

100% -> verify and measure. check the result, then compare total loop time, cost and errors against your baseline.

Jev handles the repeated choices. The deeper model handles hard problems. Verification catches bad routes before they become bad actions.
