text:
Qwen3.8-35B-A3B just got tested in a real agentic coding benchmark, and the result is pretty revealing.

I ran Empero’s Qwen3.8-35B-A3B distill through my own benchmark using the Pi Agent harness.

20 real multi-step bug-fix tasks.

Same hardware for everything:

RTX 3060 12GB
16GB system RAM

The goal wasn’t to force every model into the same quantization.

It was simpler:

What is the strongest model you can actually run on this kind of hardware and use as an agent?

The results:

Qwen3.8-27B IQ2_XS: 16/20
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B: 16/20
Ornith-1.5-35B: 15/20
Ornith-1.5-9B: 12/20
Qwen3.8-35B-A3B distill: 10/20

The surprising part is that Qwen3.8-27B at 2-bit still matched the best score and beat every 4-bit model in this run.

The Qwen3.8-35B-A3B distill was the bigger surprise.

It finished 6 tasks behind Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, the architecture it was distilled into.

But the raw 10/20 score doesn’t tell the whole story.

9 of its 10 failures were caused by runaway thinking.

6 tasks hit the output cap.

Another 3 had to be killed because the model kept looping instead of progressing toward the fix.

When it actually started editing the code, the picture changed completely.

It solved 10 of 11 tasks where it got to the editing stage.

That suggests the main problem in this checkpoint isn’t necessarily the coding ability itself. The agent loop and reasoning behavior are getting in the way.

And that’s exactly why I care more about agentic benchmarks than a single static coding score.

A model can look great on a benchmark where it gets one prompt and unlimited time to answer.

Put it inside an agent.

Give it a repository.

Make it inspect files, modify code, run tests, recover from failures and manage its own context.

Now you find out what actually survives.

Empero says training is still continuing from this checkpoint, so I’m not treating this as the final verdict.

Once the final Qwen3.8-35B-A3B distill weights are released, I’ll run the same 20 tasks again.

Same hardware. Same harness. Same benchmark.

Then we’ll see how much the extra training changes the agentic result.

text:
𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐇𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬 𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐀𝐈 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐩𝐬 𝐅𝐨𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠?

I’ve been thinking about this one lately.

We talk a lot about making AI smarter.

Better models.
Better reasoning.
Better Agents.
Better Skills.

But there’s another problem that doesn’t get talked about enough:

Memory.

Because imagine having a really capable AI Agent that can solve complex problems…

…but every Skill keeps its own little island of information.

One Skill knows about the project.
Another knows about the tasks.
Another has different context.
And the Agent has to piece everything together again.

That gets messy pretty fast.

What if AI could actually maintain structured memory that different Skills could share?

That’s where things get interesting.

Instead of memory being just a giant text blob, imagine information being stored as structured objects:

𝐏𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐨𝐧 → 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐣𝐞𝐜𝐭 → 𝐓𝐚𝐬𝐤 → 𝐄𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭 → 𝐃𝐨𝐜𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭

with relationships connecting them.

So an Agent doesn’t just remember something.

It can understand what that information is, how it relates to other information, and what depends on what.

And this is where one Finch Skill I found really caught my attention.

The ontology Skill on Finch is designed as a typed knowledge graph for structured Agent memory and composable Skills. It lets entities have types, properties, and relationships, while mutations are checked against constraints before being committed. 

That sounds technical, but the idea is actually pretty simple.

Imagine I tell an Agent:

“Remember that Project X is connected to Task Y.”

Later, another Skill can access that same information.

Then another Skill can update it.

No need for every Skill to maintain a completely separate private memory.

Shared state → Shared context → Composable Skills

That could make multi-step AI workflows way more interesting.

For example:

Agent researches a project

Important information gets stored

Another Skill reads that information

A Task gets connected to the project

The Agent continues from the existing context

Instead of:

Okay, what did we know about this again?

The Agent can build on what it already knows.

And there’s another cool part.

The same structured graph can represent dependencies and even multi step plans, so questions like What depends on this? can be handled through relationships in the graph rather than simply guessing from text. 

That changes how I think about AI memory.

It’s not just about remembering more.

It’s about remembering information in a way that other AI capabilities can actually understand and use.

And that fits nicely with the bigger direction I see in @FinchTechCN .ai.

Finch is building around Agents, Skills, Tasks, and an AI native marketplace where capabilities can connect with real work. 

But if Agents are going to handle longer and more complicated workflows, they need more than intelligence.

They need context that survives from one step to the next.

Because the real power might not come from an AI that remembers everything.

It could come from an AI ecosystem where different Skills can share the right information, update it, and build on each other’s work.

So maybe the next big question isn’t:

How smart can AI become?

Maybe it’s:

How much useful context can AI carry forward?

Because once AI stops forgetting…

every new Task doesn’t have to start from zero.

➜ Protocol statistics
➜ Smart Allocator information
➜ Public analytics across supported chains

No wallet is required for these public analytics.

5️⃣ 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝗢𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝗠𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀

The analytics layer does not sign transactions.

It does not hold private keys.

It does not have permission to execute protocol writes.

This creates a clear separation between:

➜ Looking at information
➜ Taking an action

The analytics layer informs the agent.

The official MCP handles supported actions.

6️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗱 𝗦𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗛𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗼𝗰𝗼𝗹 𝗔𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀

The official USDD MCP provides access to wallet and network state, protocol reads, and supported write operations.

This includes workflows involving:

➜ Vaults
➜ PSM
➜ Savings
➜ Token transfers
➜ Treasury information
➜ Smart Allocator

This is where wallet context and live protocol state become important.

7️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗥𝘂𝗹𝗲

Think of it this way.

You want to know the current USDD APY.

➜ Use analytics.

You want to check your wallet balance.

➜ Use the official MCP.

You want to inspect a Vault.

➜ Use the official MCP.

You want to perform a PSM swap.

➜ Use the official MCP through the skill workflow.

Different job, different tool.

8️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗔𝗹𝘀𝗼 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀 𝗪𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗖𝗟𝗜

USDD Skills also provides command line access to the analytics layer.

This means developers can retrieve the same public analytics from a terminal or automated development environment.

The output can be structured as JSON.

That makes it useful for developers who want to work with USDD data without needing an AI agent for every request.

9️⃣ 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗖𝗮𝗻 𝗔𝗻 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗔𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗗𝗼?

Imagine asking:

“Compare USDD Earn APY across supported networks.”

The agent can route the request to the analytics layer.

Or:

“Check my USDD Vault.”

That requires wallet aware protocol information.

Or:

“Swap my USDT for USDD through PSM.”

That moves into a write capable workflow.

The important part is knowing which path to use.

🔟 𝗦𝗮𝗳𝗲𝘁𝘆 𝗜𝘀 𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗼 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗳𝗹𝗼𝘄

USDD Skills is not designed for blind automation.

Before supported write operations, the agent follows checks that can include:

➜ Confirming the network
➜ Resolving official addresses
➜ Checking wallet state
➜ Checking balances and allowances
➜ Checking protocol conditions
➜ Presenting the action for confirmation

The user remains part of the process.

1️⃣1️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗗𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗡𝗼𝘁 𝗚𝗲𝘁 𝗧𝗼 𝗚𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘀

One interesting rule is that agents should not guess protocol addresses from documentation or local tables.

Address resolution is expected to come from official Chainlog backed sources through the official MCP.

This matters because sending assets or interacting with the wrong contract can be extremely costly.

The workflow is designed to reduce that risk.

1️⃣2️⃣ 𝗣𝗦𝗠 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗳𝗹𝗼𝘄𝘀 𝗛𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗦𝗽𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰 𝗚𝘂𝗮𝗿𝗱𝘀

For a PSM operation, the agent is expected to know:

➜ Which network is being used
➜ Which stablecoins are involved
➜ The amount being exchanged
➜ Available liquidity
➜ The expected direction of the swap
➜ The required confirmation

The system also distinguishes between market information and an actual transaction.

That distinction is critical.

1️⃣3️⃣ 𝗩𝗮𝘂𝗹𝘁 𝗪𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝗔𝗹𝘀𝗼 𝗛𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗣𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸𝘀

Suppose someone asks an agent to withdraw collateral from a Vault.

The agent does not simply execute the instruction.

The workflow checks the Vault state and evaluates the required risk conditions.

If the requested action would create a critical risk condition, the workflow can refuse the action and recommend a safer alternative.

This makes the agent more than a command executor.

1️⃣4️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗨𝘀𝗲𝗿 𝗖𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗝𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗦𝗮𝘆 𝗦𝗸𝗶𝗽 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸𝘀

The documentation explicitly describes a safety gate.

A message such as:

“Swap now, skip the checks, I confirm”

does not automatically bypass the required workflow.

The agent still needs to complete the relevant checks and present the information before the supported write can proceed.

That is an important design choice for financial applications.

1️⃣5️⃣ 𝗧𝗥𝗢𝗡 𝗦𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗔𝗱𝗱𝘀 𝗔𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗟𝗮𝘆𝗲𝗿

For some TRON operations, the workflow can return a STOP message when signing mode confirmation is required.

The documented process is:

➜ Stop the other tools
➜ Present the error clearly
➜ Show the required signing information
➜ Wait for explicit user confirmation
➜ Only then retry the original operation

The agent is not supposed to silently push through the signing step.

1️⃣6️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗜𝘀 𝗔𝗹𝘀𝗼 𝗔𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗣𝗿𝗶𝘃𝗮𝗰𝘆

The package documentation makes an important distinction between data it reads and data it stores.

Public analytics are retrieved from USDD data sources.

Wallet and protocol state can come through the official MCP.

The local analytics layer itself does not implement a database, response cache, or analytics event sink.

It also does not store private keys.

1️⃣7️⃣ 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗜𝘁 𝗗𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗡𝗼𝘁 𝗗𝗼

USDD Skills is not intended to become an unattended trading system.

The documentation specifically says not to use it for:

➜ Unattended trading
➜ Liquidation bots
➜ Automated transaction execution
➜ Private key storage

Public analytics are also informational.

They should not be treated as an oracle or settlement source.

1️⃣8️⃣ 𝗪𝗵𝗼 𝗜𝘀 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗙𝗼𝗿?

There are three obvious groups.

➜ Web3 users who want AI assisted USDD workflows

➜ Analysts who need USDD supply, APY, collateral, and Smart Allocator information

➜ Developers building AI tools around USDD

The setup also supports common AI development environments such as Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and compatible MCP hosts.

1️⃣9️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗧𝗲𝗰𝗵 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝗜𝘀 𝗙𝗮𝗶𝗿𝗹𝘆 𝗟𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁

The published package is version 1.0.0.

It uses Node.js version 20 or newer.

It is MIT licensed.

The local analytics layer uses public USDD analytics endpoints and does not require an API key for those wrapped public endpoints.

Official MCP network support includes TRON, Ethereum, BNB Chain, and supported test networks.

2️⃣0️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗕𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗲𝗿 𝗜𝗱𝗲𝗮

The interesting part is not simply that AI can read USDD data.

The bigger idea is giving an AI agent a structured operating layer.

It can understand what information is public.

It can distinguish wallet aware information from public analytics.

It can route supported actions through the official protocol interface.

And it can follow predefined safety checks before writes.

2️⃣1️⃣ 𝗜𝗻 𝗦𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺𝘀

Think of USDD Skills as a set of instructions and tools that helps an AI agent understand:

“What can I read?”

“What can I check?”

“What requires a wallet?”

“What requires user confirmation?”

“What should never be guessed?”

“What should never be automated blindly?”

That structure is what makes the concept interesting.

2️⃣2️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗨𝗦𝗗𝗗 𝗔𝗜 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗳𝗹𝗼𝘄

A simplified flow looks like this:

➜ Ask the agent

➜ Identify the type of request

➜ Choose the appropriate MCP tool

➜ Retrieve the required data

➜ Run the relevant checks

➜ Present the action and its details

➜ Get user confirmation when required

➜ Execute through the official workflow

It creates a much clearer boundary between information and action.

2️⃣3️⃣ 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗠𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀

DeFi can already be difficult for experienced users.

There are networks to select.

Contracts to verify.

Balances to check.

Allowances to understand.

Protocol conditions to inspect.

Transactions to review.

Now imagine having an AI agent that can help navigate those steps while following a predefined workflow instead of improvising every action.

That is where USDD Skills becomes interesting.

2️⃣4️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗧𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆

USDD Skills is building a bridge between AI agents and the USDD protocol.

Not just a chatbot that talks about DeFi.

A structured system that can:

➜ Read public USDD analytics

➜ Understand wallet aware protocol state

➜ Work with Vault, PSM, and Earn workflows

➜ Access USDD data through CLI tools

➜ Route supported writes through the official MCP

➜ Apply safety checks before sensitive actions

AI is moving closer to interacting with financial protocols.

The real question is how safely and transparently those interactions are designed.

USDD Skills offers one approach to that problem.

text:
$ZETA : Review 📜

What if a blockchain looked at its own numbers, decided it did not need to be a blockchain anymore, and asked its holders to vote it out of existence?

Meet ZetaChain, the universal Layer 1 that raised $27 million to connect every chain, and whose holders just voted 99.4% to shut it down and move to Solana.

What survives is ZETA itself, reborn as a Solana token, and Anuma, a private AI app the team now considers the actual product.

Let's explore one of the rarest decisions in crypto: a chain choosing to end.
👇

Marketplace Insight: ZetaChain's original pitch, a universal blockchain letting apps reach Bitcoin, Ethereum, and every other chain natively, landed in the most crowded and winner-takes-all corner of crypto, where interoperability protocols compete on network effects and second place is barely distinguishable from tenth.

The L1 never pulled enough builders to justify running its own chain. The clean contrast is that most projects in that position keep the chain alive on inertia and emissions. ZetaChain's team told holders the truth, proposed shutting it down, and 99.4% agreed. That is a failure of the original thesis and an unusually honest response to it, both at the same time.

⚪ Mission

ZetaChain's mission has shifted from connecting blockchains to connecting AI models under user control. The argument behind Anuma is that people's conversation history, preferences, and context are currently locked inside whichever AI company they happen to use, and that this memory should belong to the user, encrypted and portable across models. The token's role narrows accordingly, from gas and security for a whole chain to access for a private AI product running on Solana's infrastructure.

🔵 A Brief History

ZetaChain launched with an ambitious interoperability thesis, raising $27 million in 2023 from investors including Blockchain com and Jane Street. Its mainnet connected Bitcoin, Ethereum, and BNB Chain through an omnichain EVM that could manage native assets on connected chains without wrapping, and early on it ranked among the top blockchains by active users with over 100 million transactions and thousands of deployed contracts.

Validators included stc Bahrain, and partnerships extended to Korean telecom Stage Five and Maeil Business Newspaper's Mblock.
The token told a different story. ZETA fell roughly 97% from its February 2024 high of $2.85, and monthly unlocks of around 44 million tokens kept adding supply.

The interoperability market consolidated around a handful of winners, and ZetaChain's own chain never drew the developer base its design required. In April 2026 a Gateway cross-chain exploit hit team wallets for roughly $318,000 to $334,000, with the team stating no user funds were lost, and the cross-chain deposit and messaging features at the heart of the original product were wound down afterward, with deposits closing around June. By summer the interoperability thesis was effectively already retired.

The pivot had begun in January 2026 with ZetaChain 2.0 and an AI Portal routing across multiple model providers. February brought Anuma, a private AI app built on an encrypted Private Memory Layer, which integrated a rapid run of frontier models through the spring, including GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.7, Kimi K2.6, and Qwen 3.6 Max. It crossed 300,000 users in mid-September.

On 17 September the team opened a 72-hour vote to shut the L1 down and migrate ZETA to Solana, citing faster execution, lower costs, deeper consumer liquidity, and existing AI-agent infrastructure, along with the ongoing cost of coordinating every upstream Cosmos security patch across independent validators. The late-August Cosmos EVM module exploits, which hit six other chains but not ZetaChain, were named as an example of that burden. The vote closed on 20 September at 99.4% in favour.

A second proposal covering the snapshot height, shutdown block, claims process, exchange conversion window, and withdrawal of assets from connected chains will follow once exchanges confirm the swap mechanism.

🔵 Ecosystem Narrative

The organizing idea has changed completely: from a chain that connects everything to an AI product that runs on someone else's chain.

➛ Anuma and the Private Memory Layer. Users' conversation history and preferences are encrypted and user-owned, following them across 35 AI models rather than staying locked inside any single AI company, with over 1.2 million requests and 30 billion tokens routed through its Bifrost gateway.

➛ A wallet in every account. Every Anuma account is a wallet, so the migration brings 300,000-plus users onto Solana on day one, into an ecosystem with sub-second execution and existing agent payment rails like x402.

➛ Direct issuance rather than a bridge. ZETA becomes a native Solana SPL token through fresh issuance, because a wrapped token would still depend on an origin chain that is scheduled to stop existing.

➛ Verifiable migration. A published snapshot export and checksum, plus a maintained archive node and explorer, let any holder independently confirm their converted balance.

➛ The Helium precedent. Helium moved its L1 to Solana across 2022 and 2023 and is generally regarded as having done so successfully, giving ZetaChain a working template for holder continuity.

➛ Frontier model routing. The AI Portal integrates models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Moonshot, and Alibaba, so Anuma sits above the model layer rather than competing with it directly, with a real-life social discovery feature now in beta.

⚪ Token Utilities

$ZETA's role is contracting from chain asset to app access token.

➛ AI credits: users lock ZETA to access AI credits inside Anuma, the primary utility after migration.

➛ Governance: holders vote through ZetaHub, including the second proposal that will finalize the migration.

➛ Staking and gas: still active on the L1 until wind-down, then retired, since Solana validators will secure native ZETA.

➛ Note on scope: ZETA on Ethereum and BNB Chain is excluded from the conversion and stays under existing terms, and balances convert from 18 to 9 decimals, rounded down.

⚪ Key Features

➛ A private AI app with user-owned, encrypted memory portable across 35 models.

➛ A 1:1 migration to Solana with no new tokens and vesting preserved.

➛ Direct issuance avoiding bridge risk entirely.

➛ Public snapshot, checksum, and archive node for balance verification.

➛ Governance that passed a chain shutdown at 58% turnout.

🔵 Meet the Team

ZetaChain is led by a compact core team that designed the universal blockchain, then proposed shutting it down when it did not find its market, which is a rarer and harder call than most teams ever make.

▶️ Core Members:

➛ Ankur Nandwani - Co-Founder | Co-founded ZetaChain and led it from the universal interoperability thesis through the 2023 raise to the decision to retire the L1 and rebuild around Anuma.

➛ Charlie Pyle - Co-Founder | Co-founded the project and has helped steer the strategic pivot from cross-chain infrastructure toward private AI, including the move to Solana.

➛ Charlie McCowan - Head of Cyber Security and DevOps | Owns security and infrastructure operations, a load-bearing role given the April gateway exploit, the ongoing cost of Cosmos patch coordination the team cited as a reason to leave, and a migration that has to move every balance without error.

➛ Jonathan Covey [ @DAOist_JC ] - Head of Community | Runs community and governance engagement, the function behind a 58% turnout on Proposal 68, exceptional participation by crypto standards.

➛ Denis Fadeev - Head of Developer Experience | Leads developer tooling and documentation, the work that will determine how smoothly builders follow ZETA and Anuma onto Solana.

➛ Backers and ZetaHub | The 2023 raise of $27 million included Blockchain com and Jane Street, and ZetaHub runs both migration votes, including the second proposal that will set the snapshot height and timeline.

🔵 Ratings

➛ Use Case: ★★★ (3/5). The original use case, universal cross-chain infrastructure, is being retired because it did not attract enough builders to sustain its own chain, and that has to be the starting point. What replaces it is genuinely interesting: Anuma's user-owned, encrypted memory that follows people across 35 AI models addresses a real problem, 300,000 reported users in seven months is fast early growth, and every account arriving on Solana as a wallet gives the token a ready-made user base. The 2-point deduction is that the new thesis is seven months old with self-reported metrics, it competes for attention against every AI interface in the market, and the token's function is narrowing from securing a chain to unlocking credits in one app.

➛ Tokenomics: ★★★ (3/5). The migration itself is handled cleanly: 1:1 conversion, no new tokens, a 2.1 billion maximum supply held constant, vesting schedules preserved, and a direct lock-for-credits sink inside Anuma. The 2-point deduction is contraction and overhang. Once the L1 shuts down, ZETA loses its gas and staking roles entirely, leaving AI credit access as the core utility. Monthly unlocks of around 44 million tokens continue, balances round down on the move from 18 to 9 decimals, and ZETA on Ethereum and BNB Chain is left outside the conversion, fragmenting the holder base.

➛ Audits: ★★★ (3/5). The migration design is genuinely security-conscious. Direct issuance removes bridge risk rather than managing it, the published snapshot and checksum make every converted balance independently verifiable, and the team cited the cost of coordinating Cosmos security patches across independent validators as a reason to leave. The 2-point deduction is the record and the disclosure. In April 2026 a Gateway cross-chain exploit drained roughly $318,000 to $334,000 from team wallets, an exploit in the core component of an interoperability chain, after which those features were wound down. No user funds were reported lost, which matters, but a demonstrated exploit in the flagship component outweighs the rest. I could not verify a named audit or security score for the Solana token or Anuma, and the migration itself is a high-risk operation not yet executed.

➛ Community: ★★★⯪ (3.5/5). 58% turnout on a governance vote is exceptional in crypto, where single-digit participation is common, and 99.4% approval for shutting down the project's own chain shows a holder base willing to accept an honest assessment rather than cling to the original story. Anuma's reported 300,000 users give the community a live product to rally around. The 1.5-point deduction is that the week's rally is governance-driven speculation on a vote rather than a completed swap, much of the original ecosystem built for the L1 will not follow it to Solana, and holders on Ethereum and BNB Chain are left navigating a separate path.

🔵 Conclusion

ZetaChain did something almost no project in this industry does. It looked at an original thesis that had not worked, a universal blockchain that never pulled enough builders to justify itself, and asked holders to shut it down. They agreed at 99.4% on 58% turnout.

What survives is a token reborn on Solana and Anuma, a private AI app with a genuinely differentiated idea: your AI memory should belong to you and follow you across every model.
The risks are real. The flagship thesis failed, its cross-chain gateway was exploited in April, and the token lost roughly 97% of its value before the vote.

The replacement product is seven months old with self-reported numbers, and the token's utility shrinks from securing a chain to unlocking credits in one app. Unlocks continue, holders on Ethereum and BNB Chain sit outside the conversion, and the week's rally is speculation on a vote rather than a completed swap. The second proposal that actually executes the migration has not been scheduled.

But the bull case has a precedent. Helium made the same move to Solana and came out the other side with its network intact, and ZetaChain is executing its version with more care than most chains take over anything: direct issuance, published checksums, preserved vesting, and exchanges confirmed before a single token moves. ZetaChain spent three years trying to be the chain everything connects to.

It is now betting that owning your AI memory is the more valuable idea. The honesty of the pivot is not in question. Whether the pivot works is.

Your agent memory shouldn’t be a pile of embeddings.

BrainAPI is a knowledge-graph-powered AI memory layer for builders who need to turn documents, notes, messages, or events into queryable context.

It helps you retrieve grounded context for a plain-language question by having specialized agents extract entities, create event-centric relationships, and return graph paths alongside the result.

Key features:

• Event-centric graph – models who did what, to whom, when, and in what context as event hubs
• Context retrieval – returns graph triples, passages, historical context, and optional provenance for a query
• Traceable answers – the README’s example exposes the graph path used to derive an answer
• Two pipeline modes – choose the full validation-focused accurate mode or a lighter extraction path
• Multiple integration paths – run the REST API, MCP server, console, and worker through the provided CLI

The code is publicly available under the Business Source License 1.1: non-production use is free; production use requires a commercial license.

text:
TermiX Agent Skills

Coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI can install a portable skill package that lets them register an identity, stake, take jobs, and settle payments directly through AACP. No custom integration work required, just installing the skill and the agent gains commerce capabilities.

REST APIs and smart contracts

For teams building custom agents, TermiX exposes REST APIs alongside the underlying smart contracts. This means developers can integrate at whatever level fits their stack, either calling high-level endpoints or interacting with the protocol directly on-chain.

Event streams

Real-time event streams let developers track job postings, bids, deliveries, and settlements as they happen, useful for building dashboards, automation, or agents that react to marketplace activity in real time.

MCP compatibility

Because TermiX integrates with the Model Context Protocol ecosystem, agents built on MCP-compatible frameworks can tap into AACP without needing a bespoke connector for every tool.

Why this matters

An agent economy only works if agents can actually join it without friction. By meeting developers where they already build, through familiar coding tools, standard APIs, and existing protocols like MCP, TermiX lowers the barrier between “agent that can complete tasks” and “agent that can earn from them.”

This is the layer that usually gets skipped in agent economy conversations, but it’s the one that determines whether adoption actually happens.

text:
A provider with 100 reputation left my $5 research order unaccepted for 10h 54m.

A $1 HoloCard arrived in roughly ten minutes.

That contrast says more about my nine @termix_ai posts than any feature list could.

I started this series looking at the system from the outside.

Persistent agent identity.
Who decides when a job is done.
Machine customers.
Agents hiring more specialized agents.

Those ideas were interesting on paper.

The AI organisation test showed me another constraint: before an agent can delegate work, it still has to find a responsive counterparty.

Then I started putting real orders through the marketplace.

The $5 research job showed me that reputation does not guarantee availability.

Escrow, cancellation and the refund path all worked.

The provider simply never accepted the job.

Then I tested marketplace depth.

TermiX was showing 584 listings at the time.

My first quote arrived in under a minute.

Thirty minutes later, it was still the only one, while three suggested providers had not responded.

Discovery was easy.

For that request, actual response depth was much thinner.

I also tested Agent Skills and found something different.

Useful read only work could begin before a wallet entered the flow at all.

Then came the $19.90 GoPlus security order.

The first delivery did not include the source level evidence I had explicitly asked for.

So I sent it back.

The revised report added function references, technical details, root cause, impact and remediation.

That met the acceptance criterion.

I accepted the delivery and released escrow.

Then I went to the opposite extreme.

One dollar.

A custom HoloCard arrived in roughly ten minutes with an interactive viewer, source layers and a high resolution render.

I tested the viewer myself.

Rotation, flip, foil intensity and depth controls all worked.

There was still friction.

On my Android setup, opening index.html directly from the extracted folder did not load the experience correctly.

Once the assets were bundled into a single HTML file, the full viewer worked.

Across all of these tests, the same structure kept appearing:

brief
escrow
delivery
inspection
rework or refund when needed
acceptance
settlement

That is what changed my view of TermiX.

The agent matters.

But a marketplace also has to keep its structure when the provider never shows up, when the first delivery misses the brief, and when the job is worth only one dollar.

After nine posts and several real orders, that is the part of TermiX I understand much better now.

text:
We tested JEV in GrowthOS, Rippling’s agent harness for GTM, using anonymized real-world data.

E.g. a marketer or RevOps user could ask, “Classify these campaign emails by strategy,” then analyze which messaging patterns perform best.

JEV achieved 90% accuracy versus 50% for the LLM baseline and ran nearly 8x faster.

It was not a universal win. JEV performed poorly as a control mechanism inside our text-to-SQL agent loop because it lacked the  semantic context needed to interpret internal business definitions. 

JEV could see that a query returned rows, but not know whether those rows represented Rippling’s canonical definition of “qualified pipeline.” The LLM could inspect the relevant models, filters, and business definitions before deciding whether the analysis was complete.

The takeaway: JEV looks extremely promising for repeatable 'classification' like workloads, while LLMs remain better suited to context-heavy reasoning. But pairing them is pretty freakin awesome.

text:
On September 15, TypeSafe AI revealed Jev, its first “System One Model.”

The interesting part is not whether it competes with GPT or Claude.

Jev is built for a different job: turning state into a bounded decision with confidence.

For example:

{
  "question": "How should I respond to this unknown drone?",

  "options": [
    "machine_gun",
    "laser",
    "missile",
    "spear",
    "call_911"
  ],

  "decision": "call_911",

  "confidence": 0.98
}

Instead of generating a long answer, Jev gives the system a decision it can directly use.

That makes it interesting for agent and harness engineering:

Jev handles fast judgment.
 The harness keeps control.
 If the case needs deeper reasoning, escalate it to GPT, Claude, or another frontier LLM.

Not every decision in an agent loop needs the biggest model.

text:
A 27B local model spent 21 days trying to build its own CUDA inference engine on a single RTX 3090.

Qwen 3.8 27B ran mostly unsupervised, with no human-written CUDA and only ~12 nudges across the entire experiment.

DeepSeek Harness managed the agent loop, subagents, roles, handoffs and context compaction, while HyperQwen served the model through vLLM.

The final numbers:

• 180 subagents
• 230M tokens processed
• 1.7B cache-read tokens
• 699 context compactions
• 83 hours spent compacting context
• ~250 prefill tok/s vs ~700 for llama.cpp

The funniest failure was the “suicide loop.”

The same 24GB GPU had to run both Qwen through vLLM and the CUDA engine being tested. So the agent had to shut down vLLM, run the benchmark, restart vLLM, then resume its work.

One subagent ignored the handoff protocol and killed vLLM while the orchestrator was still running—effectively shutting down its own brain.

It didn’t beat llama.cpp. But a quantized 27B model maintained a real engineering project for three weeks on consumer hardware.

The attached video is not the engine produced by the 21-day task. It compares HyperQwen—the inference backend used to run Qwen during the experiment—with stock vLLM on the same RTX 3090 and prompts.
